title: The Pricing Experiment That Split the Team
summary: DevTools Co is a SaaS platform for engineering teams — it provides CI/CD pipelines, container orchestration, and deployment automation. Its customers are engineering managers who pay per seat per month.

Q1.text: A pricing experiment is live: half see $20/seat, half $25/seat. After 30 days, $20 has 15% more signups but 8% lower ARPU. What do you do first?

choices.text: Segment the results by company size and team maturity
choices.reveal: Small accounts never expand; mid-size agencies add seats for three months, then stop. The stall is segment-dependent.
choices.because: The headline numbers hide a segment-level story.

choices.text: Calculate the total revenue impact of the conversion lift
choices.reveal: 15% more signups at $20 produces $12K more MRR — but 8% ARPU drop costs $18K across existing base. Net negative.

choices.text: Interview three customers who recently signed up at $20
choices.reveal: They say the lower price was decisive — but also express concerns about missing features they'll need as they grow.

choices.text: Recommend rolling out $20/seat across the board
choices.reveal: The recommendation ignores the ARPU drop and segment differences.

Q2.text: Small teams convert 25% better at $20, mid-market shows no difference, enterprise unaffected. What do you do next?

choices.text: Model the long-term LTV of small-team signups at $20 vs $25
choices.reveal: Small teams churn at 8%/month — LTV is $340 at $20, $390 at $25. The conversion lift adds 15% more teams, each worth less.
choices.because: LTV modeling shows the trade-off directly.

choices.text: Recommend $20 for small, $25 for mid-market and enterprise
choices.reveal: The segmented recommendation is scoped — but requires tiered pricing infrastructure.

choices.text: Run a full A/B test on pricing page copy
choices.reveal: Copy variations improve click-through — but conversion to paid stays the same.

Q3.text: The net revenue impact is negative this month. What do you do next?

choices.text: Check whether small-team churn is price-sensitive or feature-driven
choices.reveal: Small-team churn correlates with lack of advanced features (SSO, audit logs), not price.
choices.because: Churn being feature-driven changes the LTV calculation — the $20 lift is genuine new revenue.

choices.text: Extend the experiment for 60 more days to confirm
choices.reveal: The extension runs — but the segment pattern is already clear at 30 days.

choices.text: Survey more customers to get additional signal
choices.reveal: More survey data arrives — but without segment analysis, responses are just a larger version of the same mixed signal.

Q4.text: LTV modeling and churn analysis both favor $20 for small teams. The question is whether to implement tiered pricing. What do you propose?

choices.text: Prioritize tiered pricing as a Q3 initiative with clear success metrics
choices.reveal: The initiative is prioritized with clear metrics: small-team conversion and 12-month LTV. Engineering estimates 6 weeks. The roadmap slot is defended.
choices.because: Prioritizing with defined metrics turns the pricing question into a testable bet with measurable outcomes.

choices.text: Accept the constraint and move forward with one price
choices.reveal: You accept the constraint — growth momentum stalls. The business case for the other workloads remains buried.

choices.text: Scope tiered pricing as a minimal change to checkout flow
choices.reveal: The minimal scope is proposed — but tiered pricing touches the billing system, and a minimal scope doesn't address customer-facing differences.

Q5.text: You've decided tiered pricing is the right strategy but engineering says it's not ready. What do you do?

choices.text: Propose an MVP with two tiers: $20 SMB and $25 mid-market, manual enterprise
choices.reveal: The MVP scopes to 4 weeks — covers the segments with real data, defers enterprise automation. The product team can ship the billing changes.
choices.because: An MVP covering the data-backed segments is better than waiting for a full solution.

choices.text: Build the full 3-tier model with custom enterprise fields
choices.reveal: The full build is scoped at 10 weeks — solves enterprise edge cases but delays the SMB change that the data supports now.

choices.text: Implement price discrimination via coupon codes for now
choices.reveal: Coupon codes handle the pricing difference — but the checkout flow doesn't explain why tiers exist. Customers report confusion.

Q6.text: Tiered pricing MVP is scoped at 4 weeks. How do you launch and measure it?

choices.text: Launch to 50% of new SMB signups and compare conversion against control
choices.reveal: The 50% cohort converts 18% better than control, retention flat. The tiered price improves acquisition without hurting retention.
choices.because: A 50% rollout with a control group isolates the pricing change's effect from other variables.

choices.text: Ship to all new signups and monitor total MRR next month
choices.reveal: MRR rises — but without a control group, you can't tell if it was the pricing change or a seasonal uptick.

choices.text: A/B test pricing page layouts instead
choices.reveal: The layout test runs — but it doesn't test the tiered pricing itself. The core question of price segmentation remains unanswered.

Q7.text: You've chosen a single price for now. But 3 months later, the plateau hasn't broken. What do you do?

choices.text: Re-run the pricing experiment with additional segment data
choices.reveal: The re-run confirms the segment pattern — small teams want $20, mid-market doesn't care. The data is now strong enough to justify tiered pricing.
choices.because: A re-run with more segment data strengthens the case for tiered pricing and removes the engineering-readiness objection.

choices.text: Survey churned customers about pricing
choices.reveal: Churned customers cite pricing among their reasons — but the survey doesn't distinguish price sensitivity from product-market fit issues.

choices.text: Offer a limited-time discount to reactivate churned customers
choices.reveal: The discount campaign runs — some customers return, but they churn again at the same rate after the discount ends. The underlying issue is unaddressed.

Q8.text: You've confirmed the segment pattern with stronger data. The C-suite wants a decision. What's your recommendation?

choices.text: Recommend tiered pricing with a phased rollout and success metrics
choices.reveal: The recommendation is clear: $20 for SMB with limited features, $25 for mid-market with full features. Phased rollout with 50% test group, success metric = net new MRR.
choices.because: A tiered recommendation with phased rollout and defined metrics turns the pricing decision into a measured bet.

choices.text: Recommend keeping $25 flat and investing in features instead
choices.reveal: The flat-price recommendation is given — but it ignores the data showing small teams are price-sensitive. The plateau continues.

choices.text: Recommend $20 flat for all segments to maximize growth
choices.reveal: The recommendation goes out — but mid-market and enterprise customers, who were willing to pay $25, leave for competitors. ARPU drops across the base.

Q9.text: The tiered pricing launches. Month 1: SMB conversion up 18%, mid-market flat. Month 2: a competitor launches at $18 flat. What do you do?

choices.text: Match the competitor's price for SMB tier, keep mid-market at $25
choices.reveal: SMB price drops to $18 — but mid-market customers see the price cut and ask why they're paying more. Internal churn rises among mid-market.
choices.because: Matching only on the threatened tier preserves mid-market value while defending the segment under attack.

choices.text: Match the competitor's price across all tiers
choices.reveal: All prices drop to $18 — total revenue drops 28% overnight. The competitor's cost structure is unknown, and you may be leaving money on the table.

choices.text: Ignore the competitor and stick with the tiered pricing research
choices.reveal: The competitor is ignored — but SMB churn rises 15% as price-sensitive customers defect. The research doesn't protect against competitive moves.

Q10.text: You matched the competitor's price on SMB tier only. What's the risk mitigation?

choices.text: Define success metrics that catch mid-market churn early
choices.reveal: The metrics are defined: mid-market NPS and churn rate tracked weekly. At the 3-week mark, mid-market churn is up 4% — early enough to adjust the positioning.
choices.because: Early churn detection on the non-discounted tier lets you react before the damage compounds.

choices.text: Offer mid-market customers a feature bonus to justify the higher price
choices.reveal: The feature bonus is announced — but features take time to build, and customers who hear about the discount can't yet see the value.

choices.text: Monitor overall MRR and hope the volume makes up for the price cut
choices.reveal: Overall MRR is monitored — but without tier-level tracking, the mid-market churn is invisible until the quarterly review.

Q11.text: Mid-market churn is up 4% at the 3-week mark. The feature bonus takes 2 weeks. What do you do immediately?

choices.text: Communicate the upcoming feature roadmap to mid-market customers
choices.reveal: The roadmap is shared — mid-market churn stabilizes as customers see the value coming. By the time the bonus features launch, churn is back to baseline.
choices.because: Communicating the roadmap buys time — customers hold off churning for features they can see are coming.

choices.text: Offer a temporary retention discount to mid-market customers
choices.reveal: The retention discount is offered — some customers stay, but the discount trains them to wait for price cuts. Renewal pricing expectations are now elevated.

choices.text: Accept the 4% churn and focus on rebuilding the feature bonus
choices.reveal: The churn is accepted — but 4% monthly churn compounds fast. By the time features launch, 8% of the mid-market base has left.

Q12.text: Mid-market churn is stabilized. The feature bonus launches next week. The board asks for a final verdict on the tiered pricing strategy. What do you report?

choices.text: Report on both the successes and the competitive-response lessons, with a revised forecast
choices.reveal: The report covers: SMB conversion +18%, mid-market churn stabilized, competitive response cost $42K in discounts. Revised 12-month forecast: $180K net new MRR, down from $210K but sustainable.
choices.because: An honest report on both wins and lessons — with a grounded revised forecast — gives the board the full picture for decision-making.

choices.text: Report the positive SMB conversion and mid-market stabilization as overall success
choices.reveal: The success story is told — but the board later discovers the $42K discount cost and the revised forecast. Trust in financial discipline erodes.

choices.text: Blame the competitor for the entire mid-market churn episode
choices.reveal: The competitor is blamed — but the board recognizes that competitive response was a choice, not a force majeure. The analysis lacks ownership.

criteria.label: Letting evidence lead
criteria.guidance: Name the segment pattern before recommending a price.

criteria.label: Sizing customer impact
criteria.guidance: Ground the decision in what changes for each segment.

criteria.label: Proving the outcome
criteria.guidance: Define the measure that validates the bet.
